lesson.subject: inquiry
lesson.title: Ask the Market
lesson.subtitle: Shark Tank | Term 4 Week 4, Session 3
lesson.footer: Shark Tank | Year 5/6 Inquiry | Week 4 Session 3

plan.curriculum: Victorian Curriculum Economics and Business, Levels 5 and 6: influences on consumer choices and how businesses find out what people want; Design and Technologies, Levels 5 and 6: investigating needs and choosing a design using criteria
plan.shape: watch, model, try: a young entrepreneur with a clear target market, fair and unfair survey questions, a quick round, then 30 minutes of the Token Test with the Grade 6s as the market
plan.criticalFeature: market research asks the people you want to sell to, with fair questions, and the team chooses from what they say, not from what the team likes best
decisionPoints: the choice check: Pocket Pal's target market
the exit board: a target market and a fair question for a new product
plan.anchor: Find a problem. Upcycle a fix. Pitch it.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 2? Say: sharks invest, they don't buy, and they use four checks. Join your team's shortlist; the Grade 6 consultant fills you in.

studentTools: A3 paper or card for three idea cards per team
manipulatives: Shark Tokens: one per Grade 5 team for each Grade 6 (about four each), cut before the session
One cup or envelope per idea card to collect tokens
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Write the three kinds of fair question: a choice question, a score out of 5, and What would make it better?
Clear desks around the room so each Grade 5 team has a stall for the Token Test
A class list with three columns: team members, final product, problem it fixes
By Friday of Week 4: send the class team list to the Shark Tank teachers
videos: Glossy Boys on Shark Tank Australia: a 13-year-old pitches nail polish for boys (youtube.com/watch?v=ie2Q1srSpk0)

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Fair survey questions, your team's survey, and your Token Test results.
resources.title: Market Research
resources.subtitle: Ask the people you want to sell to.

example.prompt: Is this question fair? You'd never leave your hat on the floor, would you?
steps: Ask: does it push people to one answer?
Would you... would you? pushes people to say no.
Pushing people to an answer makes it unfair.
example.answer: Unfair: it pushes people to one answer.

items.prompt: Sort each survey question: fair or unfair?
cards: How many days a week would you use it?
This is the best bag ever, right?
All your friends want one. Don't you?
What would you change about it?
You'd be silly not to, wouldn't you?

fair: How many days a week would you use it?
What would you change about it?
unfair: This is the best bag ever, right?
All your friends want one. Don't you?
You'd be silly not to, wouldn't you?

example.prompt: Write a fair score question about a cord tidy.
steps: Name the product: the cord tidy.
Ask for a score, not a yes.
Out of 5, how useful would a cord tidy be at your house?
example.answer: Out of 5, how useful would a cord tidy be at your house?

items.prompt: Write three fair questions for your team's survey.
rows: A choice: which of our ideas...?
answers: A choice: which of our ideas...?
e.g. Which of our three ideas would you use most?
e.g. Out of 5, how much would you want a hat clip?
e.g. What would make our hat clip better?

items.prompt: Ava wrote this survey question. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Our drink bottle sling is so cool, isn't it?
items.answer: It pushes people to say yes. Fix: Out of 5, how useful would a drink bottle sling be for you?

example.prompt: A team's results: hat clips 9 tokens, ball bags 4, cord tidy 2. Most people said hat clips need to be strong. What should they make?
steps: Most tokens: hat clips, 9.
Survey: make them strong.
Choose hat clips, and make them strong.

answers: one comment that came up a lot
one comment that came up a lot
one comment that came up a lot

items.prompt: Our final product is... Give two reasons from your results.
items.answer: e.g. Hat clips: they got the most tokens, and people said every kid loses a hat.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: read another team's results and spot what the tokens don't show.
resources.title: Extension: Read the Data
resources.subtitle: Tokens tell you a lot, but not everything.

example.prompt: Bird bath 6 tokens, seed tray 6 tokens. Is one idea the clear winner?
steps: Compare the numbers: 6 and 6.
They are the same.
The team needs more information, like the survey comments.
example.answer: No clear winner: look at the comments.

items.prompt: Team Sunrise tested three ideas. Look at the graph.

parts.prompt: Which idea got the most tokens?
How many more tokens than the key hook?

example.prompt: The book sleeve got 10 tokens, but 8 people said it is too floppy. What should the team do?
steps: The tokens say people want it.
The comments say fix the floppiness.
Keep the idea, and make it stiffer.
example.answer: Keep the book sleeve and make it stiffer, e.g. with cereal box card.

items.prompt: The dog toy got 7 tokens. Every comment said: I'd use it, but I don't have a dog. What does this tell the team?
options: the dog toy is their best idea
their market was the wrong people to ask
items.explain: They asked people without dogs. Dog owners are the target market, so they should ask dog owners.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Choose the fair question, then finish question starters for your team's survey.
resources.title: Market Research
resources.subtitle: A fair question lets people answer honestly.

steps: Our idea is great, isn't it? pushes people to say yes.
Out of 5, how useful is it? lets people choose.
The second question is fair.
example.answer: Out of 5, how useful is it?

options: You think it's amazing, don't you?
How often would you use it?
items.hint: Fair questions let people choose any answer.

options: What would you change about it?
Your mates said yes. Will you?

example.prompt: Finish: Out of 5, how useful would a ___ be?
steps: Pick the product: cord tidy.
Put it in the gap.
Out of 5, how useful would a cord tidy be?
example.answer: Out of 5, how useful would a cord tidy be?

items.prompt: Finish the question with your team's idea.
items.hint: Out of 5, how useful would a ___ be for you?
items.answer: Out of 5, how useful would a ___ be for you?

items.prompt: Finish the question with your team's idea.
Which idea got the most tokens?
items.hint: Count the tokens in each cup.
items.answer: the idea with the most tokens

resources.label: Shark Tokens
resources.description: Print and cut before the session: about four per Grade 6, one per Grade 5 team. Collect them back after.

resources.label: Family Note
resources.description: Send home at the end of the session: asks families for clean junk for the Week 6 and 7 builds.
resources.title: Shark Tank: We Need Your Junk!
resources.subtitle: A note for Grade 5 families

blocks.text: Our Grade 5s are building their own small businesses. Each team will invent a product that fixes a real problem, build a prototype, and pitch it to the Grade 6 sharks at our Shark Tank on Monday 7 December.
The big rule is upcycling: every product must be made from things that have already been used. That is where you come in.

blocks.heading: Please send in clean, safe items such as

checklist: cardboard boxes, tubes and egg cartons
clean plastic bottles, tubs and lids
old clothes, socks, jeans and fabric scraps
bottle tops, jar lids, corks and string
old toys, game pieces and broken bits that can be reused
glass, sharp metal or anything broken and sharp
packaging that held nuts or other allergy foods

blocks.text: Please send items to your child's classroom tub from Monday 2 November, and by Friday 13 November. Your child's team will tell you what their product needs.

blocks.heading: Can you help with hot glue?

blocks.text: We are looking for parent helpers to run a supervised hot glue station during the Shark Tank sessions in Weeks 6 and 7. Helpers sign in at the office and follow our school's volunteer rules, including a Working with Children Check if the school asks. If you can help, please let your child's teacher know. Thank you!

slides.notes: Session 3 of Shark Tank, the last homeroom session. One line: today the market tells each team which idea to build.

Cut the Shark Tokens: about four per Grade 6, one per Grade 5 team (12 a page, so about 4 copies per class). One cup per idea card. Clear stall space. Cue the Glossy Boys clip. Print the Worksheet one per Grade 5, a few Extension and Supported copies, and one Family Note per Grade 5.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning how market research helps a business choose what to make.
successCriteria: I can explain what market research is.
I can write a fair survey question.
I can use what the market tells us to choose our product.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Each team has three ideas. Today the market helps you pick one.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Grade 6s, you're the market today.
You'll invest tokens, just like on Shark Tank Day.
notes.prep: SC1 what market research is, reachable for all; SC2 a fair question is the core; SC3 choosing from the results. Anchor: Find a problem. Upcycle a fix. Pitch it.

slides.title: Who is Glossy Boys for?
slides.prompt: Turn and tell: who did Lucas make his product for?

notes.answer: boys and men who want to wear nail polish
beats: PLAY 0:00 to 3:00, the pitch. The player stops itself; the full clip is 10:00.
SAY: Watch for who Lucas is selling to.
ASK: Who did Lucas make his product for?
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: boys, men who want nail polish
SCAN for boys or men, not everyone.
80%+ -> cold call one pair: how would he know they want it?
Less -> replay his opening, re-ask.
SAY: Lucas got a $75,000 deal, the youngest ever to get one on the show.
He knew exactly who his customers were.
trap: saying his product is for everyone.
Fix: ask who most nail polish ads are aimed at, student names the gap.
notes.prep: Launch. A clear customer group sets up target market. The clip is an exclusive first look from Shark Tank Australia.
notes.sources: Glossy Boys, Shark Tank Australia; SmartCompany on Lucas Lane's $75,000 deal.
notes.care: Anyone can wear nail polish. Stop any teasing at once, then refocus on his customers.

slides.meaning: The group of people most likely to want your product.
slides.example: The target market for Glossy Boys is boys and men who want nail polish.

notes.answer: the group of people most likely to want your product
beats: POINT to the words. SAY: Target market. Say it with me. Tar-get mar-ket.
SAY: Your target market is the group most likely to want your product.
ASK: Pocket Pal's target market: everyone, or kids with bag hooks?
10 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: kids with bag hooks
trap: thinking the target market is everyone.
Fix: ask who would want it most, student names one group.
notes.prep: First of two key words. For most teams the target market is kids at our school, so the Grade 6s are the right people to ask.

slides.meaning: Asking your target market what they need, like and would pay for.
slides.example: Before building, the team asked 20 Grade 6s which idea they'd use.

notes.answer: asking your target market what they need, like and would pay for
beats: POINT to the words. SAY: Market research. Say it with me.
SAY: Market research means asking your target market before you build.
Then you build what they want, not just what you like.
ASK: Who should a Pocket Pal team ask?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: kids with bag hooks, kids at our school
trap: asking only your friends or your own team.
Fix: ask whether friends would say no, student names the target market.
notes.prep: Second key word. Today's Token Test is the market research.

slides.title: Fair questions get honest answers

rows: You love Pocket Pal, don't you?
Which would you use most: A, B or C?
Hats on the floor are annoying, right?
Out of 5, how useful is a Pocket Pal?
Pocket Pal is perfect, isn't it?
What would make Pocket Pal better?

slides.label: A choice. A score out of 5. What would make it better?

notes.answer: fair questions let people give any answer
beats: POINT to the Unfair column.
SAY: These push people to say yes, so they tell me nothing.
POINT to the Fair column.
SAY: A choice, a score out of 5, what would make it better. Honest answers.
ASK: Out of 5, how useful would a Pocket Pal be for you?
10 sec. Cue: fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: a spread of scores
ASK: What tells me more: a room of fives, or a spread?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a spread, it shows what people really think
trap: writing questions that start You love... or ...right?
Fix: turn it into a choice or a score, student rewrites.
notes.stretch: Why is a spread more useful than all fives?
notes.help: Give the three starters: Which would you..., Out of 5..., What would make...
notes.prep: The model for SC2. The fingers vote is live market research on Pocket Pal; read the spread aloud.

slides.title: Fair or unfair?
slides.pivot: ask: does it push people to one answer? then re-ask
slides.followUp: cold call one board: how would you make it fair?

items.text: Our hat clip is awesome, right?
items.answer: Unfair - it pushes people to say yes

items.text: Which of our three ideas would you use most?
items.answer: Fair - people can choose any idea

items.text: Would you pay $1, $3 or $5 for it?

items.answer: Unfair - it tells people how to feel

items.text: What would make this idea better?
Wouldn't your mum love one of these?
items.answer: Unfair - it pushes people to say yes

items.text: Everyone else liked it. Do you?
items.answer: Unfair - it pressures people to agree

items.text: Out of 5, how useful is this for you?

say: Your turn. Write fair or unfair.
Fair means people can give any answer.
trap: calling a question fair because it is polite.
Fix: ask whether someone could easily say no, student re-judges.
notes.stretch: Rewrite each unfair question so it is fair.
notes.help: Point to the Fair column on the last slide.
notes.prep: First decision point: spotting a pushy question. Teams write their own survey next. SC2. Eight items, about 8 minutes.

slides.title: Who should the Pocket Pal team ask?
slides.prompt: Pick the target market. Point to A, B or C.

options.misconception: thinks the target market is everyone

options.text: Kids at school with bag hooks

options.misconception: asks the people who already like the idea

notes.answer: B - kids at school with bag hooks
beats: SAY: Think about who would want a Pocket Pal most.
ASK: Who should the Pocket Pal team ask?
15 sec. Cue: voices off. Point... now.
EXPECT: B
SCAN pointing fingers, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call one B: why not the team?
Less -> ask who has the problem, then who to ask, re-ask.
REVEAL after fingers are scanned.
SAY: B. Ask the people who have the problem. Tick or fix.
trap: choosing C because the team knows the product best.
Fix: ask whether the team would ever say no, student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Second decision point. Under 80% means each team names its target market aloud before the Token Test.

slides.title: The Token Test
slides.task: Grade 5s: make an idea card for each of your three ideas, ask your fair questions and count the tokens. Grade 6s: at every stall, put one token on the idea you'd back.
slides.frame: Our final product is ___ because the market told us ___.
slides.extendedTask: the Token Test: idea cards, a three-question survey, a token count and a final product choice

notes.answer: each team chooses one product from its tokens and survey answers
beats: SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Everyone, together, on three: Ask. Count. Choose.
TIME 30 minutes: cards 8, Token Test 15, count and choose 7.
SAY: Grade 6s, while cards are made, check your team's questions are fair.
Then one token at every stall. You invest, you don't buy.
CIRCULATE. Ask: what did the market tell you that surprised you?
TIME at 30: each team writes its final product on the class list.
SAY: Name the product and the problem it fixes.
trap: a team ignoring the tokens and choosing its own favourite.
Fix: point to the count and the comments, team gives a reason from them.
notes.stretch: Extension: read another team's results and spot what tokens don't show.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: pick the fair question, finish the starters.
notes.prep: Grade 6s help count at the end and rehearse the Shark Tank Day token routine. Collect tokens back. Send the class list to the Shark Tank teachers by Friday.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: You want to sell bird feeders made from milk bottles. Who is your target market?
Write one fair question to ask them.

notes.answer: e.g. families with gardens; Out of 5, how likely are you to hang one up?
beats: SAY: A new product. Work on your own.
ASK: Name the target market, then write one fair question.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: people with gardens; a choice or score question
RECORD who writes everyone, or a question that pushes to yes.
trap: Everyone. You'd love a bird feeder, wouldn't you?
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new product. One board per student, Grade 6s included.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner your team's final product, and the evidence that chose it.
slides.selfAssessment: Fist to five: how sure is your team that the market wants your product?

notes.answer: a product and a reason from the tokens or survey
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: Fist to five: how sure is your team that the market wants your product?
5 sec. Cue: fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: mostly three to five
RECORD teams showing fists and ones for the Shark Tank teachers.
ASK: Tell your partner your final product and the evidence that chose it.
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: we got the most tokens, people said...
notes.prep: Last homeroom session. Family Note goes home today. From Week 5 the Grade 5s build with the Shark Tank teachers. SC3.
